transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-17
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood Solutions), Ethan (Boreal Head of ML), Marta (CTO), Samir (SRE), Rina (Finance)

Summary (auto): Quick session to map budget constraints to deploy options and identify pilot success metrics. Emphasis on per-token unit economics and how batching/KV cache interplay with latency SLOs.

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan, AE on the account, with Priya and Liam from the solutions team. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Ethan (Boreal): Doing good, thanks. Quick note, we're on a tight budget for Q2 so trying to understand where to land — hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:12] Priya (Redwood SE): Totally, that's exactly why we wanted to map the workloads — if you can share expected tokens per request and distribution that helps.
[00:18] Marta (CTO): We have two main workloads: an interactive assistant that needs near realtime responses, and a nightly batch QA pass that can be high throughput. Budget cap is around $12k/month for inference initially.
[00:29] Jordan: Great, that's helpful. Rough question — interactive SLO, are you targeting p95 latency sub-200ms or is 300-400ms acceptable?
[00:35] Samir (SRE): Ideally 150-200ms p95 for the assistant. Nightly can be bulk. Also must consider data residency — some PII flows to EU customers.
[00:46] Priya: Ok. So we have a couple of levers: batching to reduce per-token cost, prefix/KV cache for repeated contexts, and model quantization or smaller variants for lower unit cost. But each affects latency.
[00:57] Ethan: Walk me through how batching actually changes price — I keep hearing per-token but batching seems like magic.
[01:03] Priya: Sure. Per-token pricing is still the primary cost, but batching increases GPU utilization efficiency. For example, if you run individual requests on hosted endpoints you pay per token + overhead; with batching we amortize the kernel launch and memory copy cost across many requests. Practically that can cut per-token effective cost 20-50% depending on model and request size. But, it introduces queuing latency if you wait to accumulate a batch.
[01:24] Jordan: Also important — KV cache (we sometimes call it prefix cache) stores decoder key/values for repeated context so subsequent generations skip recomputing the prefix. For assistants with reused system prompts, that can drop token work significantly.
[01:38] Ethan: Is that available in hosted? And does it leak data or need provisioning?
[01:42] Priya: Hosted yes, we support automatic KV cache with tenant isolation. For Private/VPC you have full control and you can use your own KMS. We do keep audit logs; we talked SOC 2 earlier, we can share the pack.
[01:54] Rina (Finance): For hosted, do you have predictable monthly caps? We can't have surprise spikes.
[01:58] Jordan: Yes, we offer quotas and alerts and proposals include reserved capacity for dedicated where you commit to a baseline throughput which gives predictable per-token pricing.
[02:08] Marta: Can you ballpark per-token differences between hosted and dedicated?
[02:12] Priya: Quick thumb rules: hosted has convenience premium — think 10-30% higher effective unit cost for low-volume steady state because of multitenant overhead and on-demand scheduling. Dedicated reserved capacity reduces unit cost — especially at scale — because you eliminate multi-tenant overhead and can tune batch sizes aggressively. Private on-prem is cheapest per-token when you amortize hardware but has big ops and capex.
[02:32] Ethan: So at $12k/month what are we likely to get?
[02:36] Jordan: Depends on average tokens; if you target, say, 10M tokens/month, hosted might be tight; dedicated pilot can give better throughput for that budget. We should run simple math after you share token distribution.
[02:48] Samir: We also have concerns about cold-starts and warm warm-up costs for dedicated — do you do pre-warmed pools?
[02:54] Priya: Yes, dedicated supports pre-warm and burst pools. There's a small cost to keep GPUs warm but it stabilizes p95 latency. We can model warm-up cost into the reserved price.
[03:06] Ethan: You mentioned quantization — how mature is that on Redwood? We have some quality sensitivity for the assistant.
[03:11] Priya: We support multiple quantization profiles. For many models 4-bit quant gives 20-30% speed improvement with minimal quality loss for typical tasks, but we always validate per workload. Redwood Optimize can suggest which quant/profile to use and we can run the evals during the pilot.
[03:28] Liam (Solutions): To add, for the nightly batch you can run lower-precision variants without user-facing risk so that's a place to save a lot.
[03:35] Marta: Any mention of model fallbacks? If a peak comes and the dedicated pool is saturated, do you have graceful degradation?
[03:41] Jordan: Yes, smart routing can fall back to hosted or smaller model variants. You configure policies: prioritize latency, prioritize cost, or prioritize availability.
[03:52] Ethan: Ok let's get tactical — we can share 3 workloads: 1) assistant (avg 350 tokens, peak 120 qps, target p95 200ms), 2) nightly QA (avg 2k tokens, 10k total jobs overnight), 3) long-form summarization (avg 8k tokens, low qps).
[04:10] Priya: Good, that gives us what we need. For the assistant you'll want low-latency inference on smaller model or quantized variant with aggressive KV cache; for nightly, batch with larger model to save tokens. That mixed footprint is perfect for a hybrid pilot: run assistant on dedicated reserved pool sized for peak QPS, offload batch to cheaper dedicated instances or scheduled jobs.
[04:33] Rina: What's the pilot commitment? We're not ready to sign long-term.
[04:36] Jordan: Pilot we typically do 30-90 days with a reserved but discounted capacity for the trial. We can structure it as month-to-month reserved capacity with an exit after 60 days. Pricing tiers in the SOW.
[04:47] Samir: On the security side — we need VPC peering, SAML SSO, and KMS BYOK support. Also audit logs retention for 13 months.
[04:57] Priya: All supported. VPC peering for Private or Dedicated with private control plane, SAML SSO through SCIM, KMS BYOK for Private, and audit log export. We'll attach compliance docs.
[05:07] Marta: What's the typical ROI calculation you show to customers? We need to justify to the board.
[05:12] Jordan: Usually we show a per-token unit economics model: tokens × unit price × expected QPS plus fixed reserved cost, then compare against the in-house cost of GPUs + ops. For example, many of our mid-market customers found moving from self-host to Redwood Dedicated reduced ops burden by 60% and lowered total cost when utilization was <70% because of scheduling complexity.
[05:30] Ethan: I'm worried about the queueing latency with batching — if someone needs 150ms and you batch for 10ms to get efficiency, what happens to p95?
[05:38] Priya: Good question. Our scheduler uses latency-aware batching. You can set a max wait time per request; for the assistant we recommend small max queueing (1-5ms) and rely on KV cache and model sizing for latency. For highest consistency we recommend dedicated pre-warmed GPUs and smaller batch windows.
[05:58] Jordan: Also, you can tier traffic: high-priority traffic goes to a low-latency pool with minimal batching, and bulk to another pool. That lets you meet SLO while saving cost on the noisy part.
[06:12] Ethan: That tiering is attractive. How do we measure effective tokens saved by KV cache?
[06:17] Priya: We'll instrument a baseline during the benchmark. Typically, with repeated system prompts and user latents you'll see 15-40% reduction in token work for assistants. We'll provide tooling to compute token-level savings post-run.
[06:28] Rina: For pricing — can you give us an example matrix for our 3 workloads and $12k cap?
[06:34] Jordan: We can, but need your token distribution — once we get that we'll produce an estimated breakdown: hosted cost, dedicated reserved cost, pilot discount line items, and expected burn. We'll include burst costs and a cap guard.
[06:47] Marta: Any potential hidden costs we should be aware of? E.g., data egress, long context memory, KV storage, tracing retention?
[06:55] Priya: Data egress — if you pull logs out of region there's standard cloud egress. KV storage is small relative to model weights; we price long-term retention for caches if you need persistent caches across restarts. Trace retention is part of the observability add-on but we can include basic traces in pilot.
[07:12] Samir: We need to run an internal perf test — can Redwood run our workload on Dedicated for a day?
[07:17] Jordan: Yes, that's the benchmark we mentioned. We'll spin up a dedicated pilot pool and run your 3 sample prompts to gather real numbers. Typically takes 1-3 days to collect stable results.
[07:26] Ethan: How much instrumentation do you need from our side? We can export prompts and a simple harness.
[07:30] Priya: Just the prompts and a token distribution histogram; we'll run the harness from our side and return logs and token-level breakdowns.
[07:36] Rina: As finance I just want to confirm — pilot cost will be invoiced and applied to committed capacity if we convert?
[07:42] Jordan: Yes, standard practice is pilot invoice applied toward the first month of committed reserved capacity. We'll note that in the SOW.
[07:48] Marta: Any red flags with our EU data flow? We want EU residency for some customers.
[07:52] Priya: We support regional hosting. For EU residency we can pin model serving region and route traffic accordingly; for strict needs Private with an on-prem or VPC option is available.
[07:59] Ethan: Ok let's record the immediate next steps: we'll send token histograms and three prompts by 2/19, Redwood to send draft SOW and pilot pricing by 2/20, and schedule benchmark for 2/24.
[08:12] Jordan: Sounds good, I'll own the SOW. Priya will prepare batching/KV tuning notes.
[08:18] Priya: I'll also include quantization suggestions per workload and a short risk matrix for quality vs cost.
[08:24] Ethan: Quick clarifying question — what are the exact metrics in the benchmark output? We need p50/p95, token cost, cache hit rate, and effective tokens saved.
[08:32] Liam: We'll produce a spreadsheet with those columns and a sample row per model variant.
[08:37] Samir: One last ops question — how do upgrades/rollouts work? We can't have a breaking rollout in production.
[08:42] Priya: Rollouts are canary/A-B with automatic fallback. You can pin versions per route. We also have regression alerts tied to eval prompts.
[08:51] Marta: Ok that's reassuring.

-- intermittent channel noise and crosstalk --

[45:12] Jordan: Sorry jumped a bit — wrapping up. Recap: Redwood to share SOW/pricing, security pack, pilot plan and run benchmark. Boreal to share prompts and token distribution. Pilot targets: measure p95 latency for assistant, cost per effective token, cache hit-rate, and quality regression below defined thresholds.
[45:35] Ethan: Agreed. Also can you include a clear exit clause if the pilot doesn't meet p95?
[45:40] Jordan: Yes, we'll put pilot acceptance criteria and an exit in the SOW.
[45:44] Rina: Thanks, appreciate the clarity.
[45:46] Marta: Thanks everyone.
[45:48] Priya: We'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for the benchmark week.
[45:53] Jordan: Thank you all.
[61:58] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard acronyms (e.g. K-V cache transcribed sometimes as "K-V cash"), speaker overlap labeled where possible.
